Now that Win 10 is out, I believe Microsoft is trying its damned hardest to make sure the concerns over privacy are quashed as quickly as possible so that they can continue to collect vast amounts of data on it's consumers.

I realized I came close to believing the pro Windows 10 arguments, so I decided to go and take a look at the privacy policy for myself (I would encourage you all to do the same) and this is what I found:

https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/privacystatement/default.aspx

(make sure to click "Expand All")

First off lets look at what they collect:

There is more but these are the ones that I thought were most important

Name and contact data.

"We collect your first and last name, email address, postal address, phone number, and other similar contact data."

Seems pretty straight forward, they know where you live and who you are. Whether or not that is a good thing, is up to you.

Location data.

"We collect data about your location, which can be either precise or imprecise. Precise location data can be Global Position System (GPS) data, as well as data identifying nearby cell towers and Wi-Fi hotspots, we collect when you enable location-based services or features. Imprecise location data includes, for example, a location derived from your IP address or data that indicates where you are located with less precision, such as at a city or postal code level."

They really want to know where you are. And I mean there are Apps you use that need your location, nothing too crazy yet.

Content.

"We collect content of your files and communications when necessary to provide you with the services you use. This includes: the content of your documents, photos, music or video you upload to a Microsoft service such as OneDrive. It also includes the content of your communications sent or received using Microsoft services, such as the: subject line and body of an email, text or other content of an instant message, audio and video recording of a video message, and audio recording and transcript of a voice message you receive or a text message you dictate."

I am not trying to monger irrational fear here, if you read it, it says it collects data when the data is used in a Microsoft Service. To me that is vague, and could imply Windows itself or any app that runs on Windows. I am starting to not like this.

So what are they doing with all of this data?

If you read the section "How We Use Personal Data" It goes over the same basic usage as you would expect. They sell your data to advertisers, who use it to try and target you with ads.

This is pretty standard now days. I personally don't like it, but it is a price I am comfortable with paying for free services. Others might disagree.

Let's keep reading

Next up is the section "Reasons We Share Personal Data"

Here is where you will find that controversial line that has been floating around

"we will access, disclose and preserve personal data, including your content (such as the content of your emails, other private communications or files in private folders), when we have a good faith belief that doing so is necessary"

Right after this statement, they have a list with 4 bullet points which seem to imply that these are the 4 instances in which they would share this data, but there is no wording that says anything along the lines of "We will share this data in these cases:". It would lead me to believe that the 4 bullet points are a red herring and this "sharing data" clause is basically saying "Yes we get to Access and share your personal files whenever for whatever reason, here is a list of scenarios to distract your brain from that fact."

The disparity in numbers is not in dispute. The explanation that STEM is a woman-hating clique has become so automatic and popular, that it's worth challenging. Is it bullshit?
Low percentage of women in STEM is primarily due to misogyny amongst scientists and techies?
Completely anecdotal here, but the most vocal complaints I have heard from other women regarding STEM's misogyny come from women that avoid math and hard science courses like a plague.
That's definitely going to be true in some cases, though it's far from enough to base any general answers on, one way or the other.
The only reason why the number is so low is that very few women even try entering the field, and even fewer stick to it.

I don't know, I would ask them. A fair amount of advancements in the tech industry were made by women, and I know that the number of women in computer science has actually dropped. It's most likely a result of the dedication to a very dry subject, that most people in general don't want to do.

I don't have any sources to draw conclusions from, but I can at least throw up a few hypothesis that could potentially explain the phenomenon without resorting to the typical answer. In general, I don't like to latch onto explanations along the lines of "men and women just think too differently," because it seems very wishy-washy and culturally dependent, and it's not likely to get you anywhere. So without further ado...

Conflict of interest theory: Political establishment likes to set itself up as the center of the status quo. STEM traditionally distrusts political establishment, and has thus earned their ire. The latter would serve as explanation for both the relative lack of women, as well as the accusations of misogyny.

Barometer theory: It could be that society as a whole tends towards chauvinism, and STEM is nothing more than a very good guage of the phenomenon. In that case, it would mean that the misogyny is a very real thing, but STEM is not so much of an originator of it as an indicator.

Maturity theory: Oftentimes, I'll walk out of a presentation not because it's poorly done, but because either I know it so well that I have nothing to gain from it, or because it's so far out of my field that there's nothing for me to follow. STEM could be seeing a similar phenomenon. On one hand, it's composed of subjects like math, which are so well established and understood, that there is only so much to add. On the other hand, there's a huge volume of IT and computer fields, which are only recently achieving maturity. So in either direction, you have a situation where it takes a bit of creativity to capture people's interest.

Nerds need love theory: Like other groups with a history of facing discrimination, nerds have seen a range of bullying and out-group biases over the years, which in their case is very evident in the relative lack of female attention that the typical male nerd receives. The disparity is something to be sympathetic to rather than something to scorn. Now, with the Internet and smart devices putting nerds at the forefront, the STEM-is-misogynistic meme is a way of chickening out instead of owning up to past discrimination.

Battleground theory: Over the years, nerds have amassed a great deal of uniquely detailed, sophisticated intel on both the legitimacy and the hypocrisy of female concerns. This makes them a very valuable resource in the ongoing battle between the Warriors of Mars and the Valkyries of Venus, and both sides realize it. So among other things, they will be accused of misogyny by the Venusians to guilt them into taking their sides. And likewise, they will be accused of misogyny by the Martians in order to isolate them and keep them away from the women.

Political correctness theory: The misogyny explanation is nothing more than a politically correct interpretation of the situation. In a different social climate, people may simply point to poor levels of education, and explain the lack of women as a result of a lack of overall interest in academic fields, resulting in participation only from the people who feel most obligated to do so.

Corporate sabotage theory: The disparity might have originally been a result of a patriarchy which viewed technology as a frontier. But it was noticed, seized up, and exacerbated by big corporations who found it agreeable to have a dim-witted, pliant, infighting, dependent society devoid of true experts.

I'll add a couple hypotheses:

Isolation hypothesis:

Research often involves long periods of time with nobody to talk to (or a small working group that never changes), and many things to watch. Maybe there are more men willing to endure prolonged periods of social isolation than there are women, even though it is not the norm for either group.

Biological hypothesis:

Women have to take time off to have children. Men don't. (They probably should, but it's not biologically imperative.) When you take time off from a rapidly moving field, it takes even more time to get back up to speed, during which you're not doing useful work. This could well dissuade women who want to have children from choosing high-maintenance occupations in general. (There is evidence of this from athletics, so it's not limited to STEM.)
